item.title: Ignored for New Zealand Tests, Saransh Jain grabs seven wickets in Ranji Trophy
item.description: NEW DELHI: Saransh Jain has made the most of his return to domestic cricket after missing out on India's squad for the Test series against New Zealand. The Madhya Pradesh spinner picked up seven wickets to bowl Bihar out for just 99 in their Ranji Trophy match on Monday. Jain finished with figures of 7/40, his best bowling performance in a first-class innings. His effort left Bihar's batting line-up struggling and put Madhya Pradesh in a strong position. The 33-year-old had made his India debut in the second Test against Sri Lanka earlier this year. But he did not find a place in the squad for the upcoming two-match series against New Zealand. Bihar batters struggle against Jain Jain took seven wickets in 13 overs, giving away 40 runs and bowling one maiden. Bihar were all out for 99 in just 30.3 overs. The spinner began by dismissing Ayush Loharuka, captain Sakibul Gani and Akash Raj. He continued to trouble the batters, removing Raghuvendra Pratap Singh, Aditya Raj, Suraj Kashyap and Himanshu Singh to complete his seven-wicket haul. India debut, but no place in New Zealand squad Jain earned his first India cap at the age of 33 when he played in the second Test against Sri Lanka earlier this year. He became India's oldest Test debutant since Robin Singh in 1998. RJD Jamshedji remains India's oldest Test debutant, having made his debut at 41 years and 27 days. Jain played in the second Test (from August 23 to 27) and took three wickets. That remains his only appearance for India so far. Jain has represented Madhya Pradesh in 59 first-class matches. He has scored 2,312 runs and taken 195 wickets at an average of 28.23.

item.title: His dad died building the stadium. The Brewers gave him World Series tickets
item.description: Roland "RJ" Wischer and his wife Betsy told their two children they were going to Game 2 of the World Series , but it was different for them. They explained the Milwaukee Brewers making it this far was rare and they would be witnessing a historic Wisconsin sports moment . They also explained why the Brewers gave their family tickets for free. "I tell them, mostly, that we're there because of their grandfather," Wischer said. "Their grandpa gave his life building this stadium." More: When do the Brewers play next? Game 3, World Series schedule Their grandfather, Jeffrey Wischer, died in 1999 during construction of then-Miller Park, now American Family Field . Jeffrey Wischer died along with William DeGrave and Jerome Starr when a crane known as Big Blue collapsed while raising a piece of the stadium roof amid high winds. It's among the darkest days in Brewers history, one that is immortalized with a statue of the three men in the shadow of the ballpark. Roland "RJ" Wischer said the Brewers have invited him and his family back to the ballpark multiple times to honor his father, alongside DeGrave and Starr. He was at the inaugural game in 2000, he came back last year to remember the 25th anniversary of the tragedy and he's been to other regular season games over the years. But last week, Wischer said the ironworkers union reached out to him to see if he would be willing to talk to the Brewers. He agreed, and the team called and offered him four free tickets to Game 2 of the World Series at American Family Field, where the Brewers would face the Tampa Bay Rays. "The Brewers have been really good to me. Really, really good to me," Wischer said. "I wasn't really expecting it. It wasn't the phone call that I was expecting." Becoming an ironworker Growing up, Wischer spent a lot of time with his mom. His dad was often away working jobs on weekends and holidays. "There was a time in my life that I was frustrated over the fact that I didn't get time with him and that I didn't remember him," he said. Wischer was about 8 years old when his dad died. He doesn't have many memories of him, but remembers him as "stern but fair." "He had his set ways that he liked things done," Wischer said. "If there wasn't the lines in the carpet from the vacuum when he got home, you clearly didn't vacuum. He liked things a certain way. He was strict but he was a good dad." He talked to one of his dad's old friends about being an ironworker. "I didn't realize it until I became an ironworker that when you are trying to provide as much as you can for your family, if there's shutdown work over the weekend or on a holiday and you're going to make time-and-a-half or double-time on those projects, you're going to go on those projects and sacrifice the time with your family," Wischer said. item.description: Brighton boss takes aim at Liverpool performance Fabian Hürzeler questions Liverpool approach after Brighton suffer Anfield defeat Fabian Hürzeler left Anfield convinced Brighton had missed an opportunity, arguing that only one side had truly sought to create during Liverpool’s 2-0 victory. The Brighton manager’s pointed assessment followed a match settled by a Pascal Gross own goal and an Alexander Isak finish. His side had more possession and a higher expected goals tally, according to Beth Lindop’s report for ESPN, but Liverpool secured the points and a clean sheet. Yet Hürzeler’s frustration came with an acknowledgement of what the hosts had done well. Liverpool protected their penalty area, blocked shots and made the decisive moments count. Those qualities helped Andoni Iraola’s team record a fourth consecutive victory in all competitions. IMAGO | Anfield Index Hürzeler makes pointed claim over Liverpool approach “I think everyone in the stadium saw that there was one team who really tried to create and try to win this game and therefore I have to praise my players,” Hürzeler said. It was a forceful defence of Brighton’s performance, rather than a description Liverpool would necessarily recognise. The visitors’ possession and chances gave their manager grounds to feel disappointed, but they did not produce a goal. Hürzeler also disputed the suggestion that Brighton only threatened once Liverpool had established their advantage. “Also, before they scored, we had one, two big chances and today I think it was just the difference that they scored, we didn’t score.” His argument centred on the opportunities Brighton failed to take. The outcome, in his view, did not reflect the promise of their attacking play. Liverpool defending earns Brighton manager’s praise Despite questioning Liverpool’s approach, Hürzeler was clear that their defensive work contributed to the result. “They kept a clean sheet because they defended well with their centre-backs, with full-back Araujo and with Kerkez,” he said. “I think they blocked a lot of shots. item.title: 'I genuinely thought I was going to die': Ex-Australia cricketer Usman Khawaja reveals career-long health secret
item.description: Former Australia opener Usman Khawaja has revealed that he battled rheumatoid arthritis throughout his international cricket career, keeping the condition hidden from his teammates for years. Speaking on ABC, the 39-year-old recalled being diagnosed with the illness at just 22, when severe pain in his left knee made even walking difficult. “I genuinely thought I was going to die,” Khawaja said, describing how he went from being an athletic cricketer to someone who could barely walk 10 metres. He was diagnosed in 2009 while playing for New South Wales during the off-season. Although doctors and cricket officials knew about his condition, he chose not to tell his teammates. Why Khawaja kept his illness secret Khawaja feared that revealing his health problems could be used against him, and he did not want people treating him differently. As a result, even former teammates David Warner and Michael Hussey were unaware of his condition. He relied on regular medication and injections to control the disease and returned to cricket around six months after his diagnosis. The treatment played a crucial role in helping him continue his career. "Without that drug, I would never have played cricket ever again or even lived a normal life again,” he said. Khawaja hopes his experience will encourage people living with autoimmune diseases to keep pursuing their goals. “If a person can play at the top level as a professional cricketer with rheumatoid arthritis, then I think a lot of other people can achieve a lot, too,” he added. Khawaja's cricket career and lasting message Khawaja made his Test debut against England at the Sydney Cricket Ground in January 2011. Despite being dropped from the team several times, he made important comebacks. One of his biggest achievements came during the 2021-22 Ashes, when he scored centuries in both innings of the Sydney Test. He retired from Test cricket in January 2026 after the fifth Ashes Test against England in Sydney. He finished with 6,229 runs and 16 centuries in 88 Tests. Khawaja is also preparing to share more about his life and career in his upcoming autobiography, Sabr . His story highlights the health struggles that can exist behind the success of professional athletes. By speaking publicly about his illness after retirement, Khawaja hopes to raise awareness about rheumatoid arthritis and show others that a chronic condition does not necessarily mean giving up on their ambitions.

item.title: Hansi Flick reveals why Barcelona star Raphinha requested El Clasico substitution during Real Madrid defeat
item.description: FC Barcelona v Real Madrid - LaLiga EA Sports 2026/27 - Getty Images Sport Barcelona manager Hansi Flick has revealed that Raphinha asked to be substituted moments before Real Madrid scored their late Clasico winner. The Brazilian attacker, who had been struggling with a recent injury issue, completely ran out of energy during the closing stages of the match. Late heartbreak for Barcelona Barcelona suffered a frustrating 2-1 defeat against Madrid in Liga on Sunday afternoon. The team conceded the decisive, match-winning goal in the 87th minute to lose the closely contested Clasico. The heartbreaking late goal arrived just one minute after star forward Raphinha was substituted. The Brazilian attacker has been in phenomenal domestic form, registering an impressive 13 goals in nine Liga appearances this season. However, his completely unexpected departure from the pitch was not a deliberate tactical decision made by the manager. Flick reveals tactical shift abandoned Flick had entirely different tactical plans for the closing stages of the high-stakes match. The manager wanted to use the 29-year-old in a more withdrawn, central position to push for a late victory. That attacking plan was ultimately abandoned when the player clearly communicated his physical struggles directly to the coaching staff on the bench. "We wanted to play in the last minutes with Raphinha as a number 10, but he asked us to take him off," Flick explained during his post-match press conference. International break takes its toll Raphinha simply did not have the physical capacity to finish the incredibly demanding domestic fixture. He picked up an injury problem during the recent international break and consequently lacked the required energy levels. Flick confirmed to the gathered media that the attacker was completely exhausted by the time he approached the touchline and requested the change. "He couldn't play anymore," the Barcelona manager stated bluntly when discussing the Brazilian winger's physical condition in the final moments of the game. Barca will monitor Raphinha's condition The medical staff will need to carefully monitor his ongoing recovery following the initial injury sustained during the international break. Flick will be desperately hoping his star attacker can fully recover his energy reserves to maintain his incredible league goalscoring form in the coming weeks.

item.title: Three things we learned from the United States Grand Prix
item.description: Mercedes' Italian driver Kimi Antonelli (RONALDO SCHEMIDT) Kimi Antonelli stands at the threshold of Formula One's hall of fame, needing just two more points to become the sport's youngest champion and first Italian for 73 years. His commanding triumph in Sunday's United States Grand Prix was acclaimed as "his best so far" by Mercedes team boss Toto Wolff, endorsing his talent again and proving that the 'silver arrows' remain the team to beat. With five races remaining, AFP Sport looks at three things we learned from the 20-year-old Italian's ninth win of an outstanding season: Antonelli maturing fast and adding strategic authority to his arsenal A brief comparison with the misfortunes and struggles of his teammate and nearest rival George Russell reveals how rapidly Antonelli has developed from a daring precociously talented kid into a maturing competitor. Team chief Wolff, having seen him deliver staggering wins in Monaco and Monza, called Sunday's success "the race of a champion who isn’t the champion yet". It is as if his passage from teenager to twenty-something has taken him into a higher level of authoritative and complete racing –- adding a strategic dimension to the raw pace that set him apart. While the luckless Russell, who began the season as favourite for the drivers' title and won the opener in Australia, laboured to eighth – the minimum required to keep alive his academic title fight – Antonelli skated home on the same one-stop strategy. Hampered by an early and harsh five-second penalty, Russell admitted he could not deliver the pace, or panache, needed. Before the race, Antonelli had called on Woff in his office. "He comes in, sits on my chair, feet up, and chats away saying 'this is so funny – I'm not thinking about the championship at all!' in a kind of youngish excitement, like it's surreal." Wolff added that this approach to such a major day in his embryonic career was "innate in him and not something to be trained for". Antonelli himself recognised this win as better than Monza, where he was 19th on the grid, because of how he and his crew developed performance through the weekend and executed their bold strategy after seizing pole. Wolff said the team's update was difficult to manage for the drivers, adding that Antonelli's style "just glues with the car" while Russell "just struggled so much".
